implementation_notes: threading.Condition bundles the lock and the wait set, and wait_for() automates the predicate loop - the documentation defines it as roughly while not predicate(): cv.wait(), evaluated with the lock held - so the classic structure is reduced to one library call, which is why Python code should reach for it instead of a hand-written flag and notify. The lock must be held on entry (use the condition as a context manager) and notify/notify_all must also be called with the lock held; use queue.Queue when the guard is literally 'an item is available', and asyncio.Condition for the same suspension in async code (not thread-safe).
pitfalls: Calling wait/wait_for or notify/notify_all without holding the condition's lock raises RuntimeError at runtime, not at import time.
notify() wakes one waiter; with several threads waiting on different predicates notify_all() is the safe default and the documentation says so.
Long work inside the guarded region serializes every waiter, because the lock is held for the whole critical section.

variants.name: queue.Queue blocking get/put (bounded handoff)
variants.implementation_notes: queue.Queue is the library form of the guard: get() blocks while the queue is empty and put() blocks while it is full (with block=False and timeout= variants raising Empty/Full), the module is documented as the thread-safe way to exchange data between threads, and Queue.shutdown() (3.13) can wake blocked callers. Prefer it whenever the predicate is items-or-space available; keep Condition for guards over state that is not queue-shaped, since a queue cannot express 'the device is ready'.
pitfalls: An unbounded queue (maxsize<=0) silently removes the 'space available' half of the guard, so backpressure disappears.
There is no close(): shutdown needs a sentinel value or a flag plus a timeout on get(), otherwise consumers block forever.

variants.name: asyncio.Condition.wait_for (single event loop)
variants.implementation_notes: asyncio mirrors threading with primitives that suspend the task instead of the thread: asyncio.Condition combines a lock and an event, wait() releases the lock and suspends, and wait_for() repeats wait() until the predicate holds (the documentation warns a task may return from wait() spuriously). The primitives are explicitly not thread-safe and take no timeout argument, so use asyncio.wait_for() around the wait and asyncio.Queue when the guard is item-availability; mutating the guarded state from another OS thread requires loop.call_soon_threadsafe.
variants.code_sketch:
import asyncio

cond, items = asyncio.Condition(), []

async def take():
    async with cond:                          # acquires the underlying lock
        await cond.wait_for(lambda: items)    # suspends the task, not the loop
        return items.pop()
async def put(x):
    async with cond:
        items.append(x)
        cond.notify()
pitfalls: asyncio primitives are not thread-safe: touch the guarded state from a worker thread only through loop.call_soon_threadsafe.
A blocking call inside the guarded region stalls every task, including the notifier - use awaitable I/O only.
